Perhaps the gravest violence we can do to ourselves is to live out our lives believing the world to be a fixity handed down to us by the authorities of history and life to be a matter of taking immutable givens. Daring to believe otherwise — to believe that even our smallest purposeful action alters the monolith of reality in some subtle, meaningful way — is an act of courage and resistance, an act of immense vulnerability to the possibility of disappointment, vulnerability the commonest cowering from which is cynicism.

James Baldwin knew this when he issued his lyrical and impassioned insistence that “nothing is fixed, forever and forever and forever, it is not fixed,” that “we made the world we’re living in and we have to make it over.”

Hannah Arendt knew this when she considered how we invent ourselves and reinvent the world, observing that “the smallest act in the most limited circumstances bears the seed of boundlessness, because one deed, and sometimes one word, suffices to change every constellation.”

Richard Powers knew this when he made his contribution to Take My Advice: Letters to the Next Generation from People Who Know a Thing or Two (public library) — artist and writer James L. Harmon’s wonderful 2002 anthology of wisdom from stellar minds, a decade in the constellating, envisioned as an eclectic contemporary counterpart to Rilke’s timeless Letters to a Young Poet, which had moved Harmon deeply when he first encountered it as a young man.

Two decades before Powers won the Pulitzer Prize for his sylvan symphony The Overstory, he echoes Seamus Heaney’s exhortation to always remain “true to your own secret knowledge” and writes:

Never forget what you were born knowing. That this fluke, single, huge, cross-indexed, thermodynamic experiment of a story that the world has been inventing to tell itself at bedtime is still in embryo. It’s not even the outline of a synopsis of notes toward a rough draft yet. Buy the plot some time.

We buy the plot time with the currency of our conscious choices, the grand and the mundane alike — the daily actions that make us what we are, the people who make the world what it is. Powers writes:

Take in more, consume less, recycle everything; book-keep all hidden costs; find out where you have been set down; lobby for a smaller market; get rid of your car and travel as widely as you can (yeah, walk: what the hell); try to say a little more than you mean; carry a pocket encyclopedia (ask for one without packaging) and when the entry on “Diffusion Constant” says, “for more information, see ‘Pastry War,'” see “Pastry War.”

This latter sentiment might at first appear dated in the hindsight of two decades, in the epoch of Wikipedia. But it is actually all the more insightful and urgent today, for the quiet act of resistance at its heart has grown all the harder. What I most rue about the internet is that, for all its riches of readily accessible information, it has altered the texture of human curiosity, vanquishing that wondrous encyclopedic feeling of learning about the thing you hadn’t known you didn’t know but now greatly enjoy knowing. Somewhere along the way of choices being made for us by an insular tribe of technologists, discovery was sacrificed at the altar of search as algorithms perfected the mechanics of giving us more and more of what we already knew we wanted and believed, rendering the mind itself more and more a fixity. Would you be Googling “Pastry War” now had I not made this point about a point Richard Powers made long ago on the pages of a yellowing book I pulled from my bookshelf by some incomputable human impulse this morning?

Those choices matter, Powers reminds us, even at the smallest scale. There is no fulcrum too small for the lever of change to lift from, but the lift must begin with lucidity. He writes:

Take a full look at the worst. Acknowledge the figures: the runaway birthdates, the irreversible extinctions and ruined habitats, the meaningless economies fueled by waste, the exported shooting wars and their cover causes… Then work at whatever comes to hand. Useful or not, it makes no difference. Jumping in is the only calculus that emergency ever allows.

Complement with Rebecca Solnit on rewriting the world’s broken stories with our actions, then revisit What If — a wondrous French picture-book about daring to imagine and build a different world for the children of tomorrow.

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If it makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider aiding its sustenance with a one-time or loyal donation. Your support makes all the difference.

#9068. What Happens When Elders Share Their Stories

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

When I moved from the San Francisco Bay Area to a small, rural town in Vermont, I wanted to find a way to contribute to the local community. Knowing there was a significant senior population here, I reached out to the town librarian with hopes of helping elders share their stories.

The local historical society took interest in this idea, which led to an exhibit at the 159-year-old Tunbridge World’s Fair, and a book series entitled Folk Life: Tunbridge Oral Histories. The first two print runs sold out. The second collection of stories has just been published, and people are already asking who will be featured in the third.

What is it about life stories that strikes such a universal chord? And why is it important—and even imperative—to share our stories with others? I interviewed oral historians, teachers, and a digital storyteller to discover more about why the age-old tradition of recording oral histories continues to make such a significant impact for individuals and communities.

Storytelling is, according to scientific research, a biological shortcut to human connection. Uri Hasson and fellow researchers at Princeton University discovered that the brains of the storyteller and listener physically sync up while a story is being told, promoting social connection, trust, and empathy.

The more emotionally affecting the story is, the stronger this connection becomes. As emotions and tension rise, hormones are released, including oxytocin, the “bonding hormone”; dopamine, which sharpens focus; and cortisol, which promotes attention and alertness as conflicts in the story arise. These hormonal responses enhance both the listener’s memory and connection to the storyteller.

For Erin Barnaby, a digital storyteller and 11th-generation Tunbridge native, oral histories create a connection not only to people, but also time and place. “My dad recently sold his house to my uncle, a house that he built on land that my grandfather had given to him. I love to hear him tell stories about the shifting of the land, from sheep farms to dairy farms and the shift from open pastures to forests.”

Even when the subject matter might not be instantly relatable, the process of listening to another’s stories still creates a profound interpersonal connection. Esther Ehrlich, who worked at UC Berkeley’s Oral History Center for six years before launching an oral history business of her own, experienced this sense of connection firsthand:

I was assigned an interview with a former medical malpractice insurance guy, which initially didn’t interest me at all. And then lo and behold, after interviewing this man, I found him absolutely fascinating. What I came to discover was that by the time we were done, or even partway in, I came to love every single person I interviewed. I would feel connected to them and them to me.

From that biological and psychological basis, oral histories make a critical social contribution.

According to the Oral History Association, “oral history is the oldest type of historical inquiry, stemming from the oral traditions of myriad cultures across the globe, predating even the written word.” These personal stories expand upon the narratives of history books, allowing people from varied walks of life to share their unfiltered experiences and perspectives. Indeed, many works by trained historians rely on oral histories.

The founders of Voice of Witness, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing human rights by amplifying unheard voices, believe that oral history “can democratize history, contribute to narrative change, and illuminate issues and events in a profoundly powerful way.” Enabling individuals to safely share their stories opens people’s minds to fresh perspectives and vantage points.

While oral histories are limited to an individuals’ memories and are by nature subjective, they remain incredibly valuable in their ability to paint a portrait of time and place. Plus, their narrative-driven format brings history to life in a more memorable way than date- and fact-focused textbooks.

Helen Marks, a former history teacher who has spoken to thousands of students about her experience as a hidden child in Belgium during World War II, has observed that when a person shares their stories, it brings that part of history to life:

I am among the few surviving hidden children who are willing and able to talk about their experiences in the Holocaust. Reading numbers on a page does not create the same impact as someone standing or sitting in front of you describing a moment that was frightening or was so foreign they didn’t know what to do. . . . I think that when you connect a face, no matter what the face looks like, you get a wholly different reaction than when you read a page full of facts.

Throughout the interviews I conducted for Folk Life, the importance of leaving a meaningful legacy was a common theme. “That’s the reason we share our stories,” says Marsha Higgins, a history teacher for nearly 40 years. “It makes us feel like we matter.”

Higgins taught students to create personal narratives from a young age. Decades later, former students still express their thanks for her guidance in teaching them the importance of recording their experiences.

“I encouraged students to write down things that happened to them. It’s helpful to know at the time, you’re creating chapters in your life, that your story is just as interesting as anybody else’s.”

Like Marks, Higgins grew up around immigrants from Europe. “And they all had stories,” she says. “Whenever we got together, somebody would tell me a story. How do you make conversation without one? It’s just so much a part of who we are.”

“I think everyone wants to know that they have made a positive difference,” says Marks. “That they did some good, that their being here wasn’t just a fleeting moment of nothingness, but that they contributed something. They reacted to something. They gave something. So when you tell stories, that’s where you learn about people and what they value.”

Neal Allen, a coach and author (most recently of Good Writing: 36 Ways to Improve Your Sentences with his wife Anne Lamott), spent several years as a hospice volunteer. During that time, he helped a number of people share and record their stories.

“Every week I had one or two clients who were dying, and I spent time fluffing their pillows, listening to their stories and how they approach death. The funny thing is we were always asked, ‘Oh, isn’t that hard?’ It was quite the opposite. It was really quite extraordinary.”

A seasoned journalist, Allen knew how to ask evocative questions. “Oddball memories were coming up that hadn’t come up in 50 years maybe,” he says, which led to more and more stories. “My subjects would get really involved in it. To finish their story, it would take eight to 12 hours, sometimes up to 40 hours.”

Allen wrote a biography about his father, which proved to be a learning opportunity for both him and his brothers:

Once [the book] was bound and we read it all the way through, we had the same reaction, ‘Oh, I didn’t know he had done this. Oh, I didn’t know he had done this. Oh, did you know about that?’ Our second reaction was, ‘We’re not in it,’ and burst out laughing. It was easy to laugh about because he never, ever gave us any sign that he disapproved of us in any fundamental way.

For older adults, sharing stories not only connects them with family, each other, and audiences, it also exercises the brain and fosters a sense of well-being. Story sharing activates memory networks while encouraging reflection on past experiences.

Reminiscence therapy, a structured method of helping individuals recall, organize, and share life stories, has proven helpful in elevating people’s moods, enhancing their self-esteem, resolving conflict, and promoting meaning. This mode of therapy is becoming increasingly popular as a way to support seniors facing cognitive decline as well as mental health challenges.

Ehrlich notes that more than ever, hearing or reading about others’ stories is a powerful tool for building bridges, especially in this divisive climate.

“We have so much more in common than not,” she says, noting that “there’s a desperate need to understand each other better. Oral history is perhaps a tool for seeing beyond our rigid ideas of who people are and breaking through into a fuller understanding.”

“What always astonished the subject of the memoirs was how many people they had touched,” says Allen. “I think we touch a far greater number of people than we can hold or remember at any one time.”

In this way, sharing stories reminds us that our interactions have more of an impact than we realize, not only in our close-knit circles, but also at work, at school, and even in everyday exchanges.

What sharing our stories boils down to, Ehrlich believes, is that it’s a fundamental human instinct:

How do we live a life? How do we deal with joy and difficulty and disappointment and pleasure? How do we make choices? What do we have control over? What don’t we have control over? Oral histories, at their most basic, include all the stuff that makes us people, including our desire to be seen, heard, and understood. And everybody’s stories matter.

Elisse Gabriel is a senior writer and editor, with clients ranging from schools, museums, and nonprofits to national retailers, tech startups, and Fortune 500 companies. Currently, she is working on a middle grade novel that celebrates the superpower of sensitivity in boys.

According to an analysis of 99 studies, mental well-being leads to a longer life.

Body changes or chronic illness can disrupt our sense of meaning and challenge our identity, purpose, and assumptions about the future.

You can be good at your job and still feel a lack of engagement, challenge, and meaning.

Do you have a long-term goal that's meaningful to yourself and the world?

What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.

What if you could fall in love, or forge deep connections, in just 45 minutes? Our guests, Kristen Meinzer and Jolenta Greenberg of By The Book podcast, try out 36 questions with their partners to see if they can strengthen their connection.

The Greater Good Science Center studies the psychology, sociology, and neuroscience of well-being, and teaches skills that foster a thriving, resilient, and compassionate society.

#9067. The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD

The brain has a remarkable ability to recognize danger, but new research suggests that this survival mechanism may also explain why people sometimes feel threatened in situations that are actually safe. The discovery offers a possible explanation for the intense fear responses associated with anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

For years, scientists believed that fear helps the brain distinguish more clearly between threatening and harmless experiences. However, a study led by researchers at the Douglas Research Centre at McGill University and the University of Toronto-Scarborough challenges that assumption. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest that fear may have the opposite effect.

In experiments involving mice, researchers trained the animals to associate one environment with danger and another with safety. Instead of developing increasingly separate neural representations of the two locations, the animals' brain activity began to show overlapping patterns. In other words, the brain's representations of safe and dangerous experiences became less distinct.

"Our findings suggest fear may blur the boundary between danger and safety rather than sharpen it," said senior author Mark Brandon, Associate Professor in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and Researcher at the Douglas. "This could reshape how scientists think about anxiety and PTSD."

How Scientists Watched the Brain Process Fear

To investigate how these changes occur, the research team developed an unusual experimental setup that combined augmented reality with real-time brain imaging.

The researchers created a specialized arena in which mice could be virtually "teleported" between environments associated with danger and safety. By changing the sights and sounds surrounding the animals, scientists could make them experience different settings without physically moving them to another location.

At the same time, miniature microscopes monitored hundreds of neurons in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. This allowed the team to observe how the brain's activity changed as the mice transitioned between experiences associated with safety and threat.

"That gave us something conventional fear conditioning experiments cannot easily provide: a moment-by-moment view of the brain switching between competing maps of dangerous and safe memories," said Robert Rozeske, Assistant Professor in University of Toronto's Department of Psychology and lead author on the publication.

Why the Brain May Confuse Safety With Danger

Although mixing memories of safe and dangerous experiences might seem like a problem, the researchers believe it could serve an important evolutionary purpose.

The experiments suggested that overlapping memory representations allowed the brain to retrieve information about previous threats more rapidly. This could help an animal recognize possible danger and respond before it is too late.

Such a strategy comes with a trade-off. By prioritizing speed over accuracy, the brain may react to a potential threat even when the current situation is harmless. From a survival perspective, responding unnecessarily to a false alarm may sometimes be preferable to overlooking a genuine danger.

"The ventral hippocampus may be part of a system that prioritizes a rapid 'better safe than sorry' response," said Rozeske. "In other words, the brain may sacrifice precision for speed when danger matters."

The ventral hippocampus is a part of the hippocampus involved in processing emotionally significant experiences, including fear and anxiety. The new findings suggest that overlapping memory representations in this region may help the brain switch rapidly into a defensive state.

A Hidden Survival Mechanism May Help Explain PTSD

The discovery could also offer insight into why people with anxiety and trauma-related disorders sometimes experience powerful fear responses in situations that pose no immediate threat.

For someone with PTSD, an otherwise harmless sight, sound, or environment can trigger memories associated with a traumatic experience. The resulting fear can feel immediate and overwhelming, even when the person is objectively safe.

The researchers suggest that such reactions may arise, at least in part, when a normally useful survival mechanism becomes excessively sensitive. Instead of reflecting a system that has simply stopped distinguishing between different memories, these responses might involve a brain mechanism that shifts too quickly from recognizing safety to anticipating danger.

"Our study suggests that's not necessarily a broken pattern-separation system, but possibly an overactive version of a normal survival mechanism gone into overdrive," said Brandon. "That reframing could guide therapeutic approaches to address an overly fast transition to 'danger mode'."

Because the experiments were conducted in mice, additional research is needed to determine whether the same mechanisms contribute to anxiety and PTSD in humans. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new way to understand how fear influences memory and why a brain system designed to protect against danger might sometimes generate fear when no immediate threat exists.

The study, "Overlapping representations in the ventral hippocampus support rapid fear memory retrieval," by Robert Rozeske and Mark Brandon, was published in Nature Neuroscience.

The research received support from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada.

Materials provided by McGill University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9066. How to Bear Your Desolations

The morning after a relationship of depth and significance long bending under the weight of its own complexity had finally broken with an exhausted thud, I opened the kiln to discover a month’s worth of pottery shattered — two pieces had exploded, the shrapnel ruining the rest. All that centering, all that glazing, all the hours of pressing letterforms into the wet clay — all of it in shiny shards. And meanwhile spring was breaking outside and a little girl in bright blue rain boots was jumping in a puddle, smashing the reflections of the clouds with savage joy.

And I thought, this is all there is: breaking, breaking apart, breaking open.

It is not an easy assignment, being alive. Coming awake from the stupor of near-living that lulls us through our days, awake to the knowledge that on the other side of the neighborhood ICE trucks are handcuffing people and on the other side of the planet children are dying in gunfire, while outside the first birds of spring are singing and everywhere people are falling in love and in some faraway mountain village a shepherd is singing under a thousand stars. And somehow, somehow, all of it has to cohere into a single world in which we, in all our incohesion, must live this single life.

Ellen Bass reckons with all of this in her splendid poem “Any Common Desolation,” originally published in The Academy of American Poets’ poem-a-day newsletter and later included in James Crews’s lifeline of an anthology How to Love the World: Poems of Gratitude and Hope (public library), shared here with Ellen’s blessing.

can be enough to make you look up at the yellowed leaves of the apple tree, the few that survived the rains and frost, shot with late afternoon sun. They glow a deep orange-gold against a blue so sheer, a single bird would rip it like silk. You may have to break your heart, but it isn’t nothing to know even one moment alive. The sound of an oar in an oarlock or a ruminant animal tearing grass. The smell of grated ginger. The ruby neon of the liquor store sign. Warm socks. You remember your mother, her precision a ceremony, as she gathered the white cotton, slipped it over your toes, drew up the heel, turned the cuff. A breath can uncoil as you walk across your own muddy yard, the big dipper pouring night down over you, and everything you dread, all you can’t bear, dissolves and, like a needle slipped into your vein — that sudden rush of the world.

Complement with Henry James on how to stop waiting and start living and Hermann Hesse on how to be more alive, then revisit Ellen’s magnificent poem “How to Apologize.” And if you are looking to break your poetry open, I couldn’t recommend her Living Room Craft Talks more heartily.

#9065. Kandinsky record and trove consigned by Jeff Koons buoy Christie’s 20th-century sale in New York

Adrien Meyer selling Kandinksy's Betonte Ecken (1922-23) for $74m (with fees) at Christie's 20th-century evening sale on 17 November 2026 in New York

Buoyed by a handful of gems, Christie’s 20th-century evening sale on 17 November in New York racked up $521m, or $627m with fees, underscoring the allure of rare-to-market trophy works.

The hammer total hit the low-side of the $511m-$743m pre-sale estimate (all estimates calculated without fees). The result was a marked improvement on last November’s equivalent sale, which made $390.1m, or $471.7m with fees.

Thirty one of the 75 lots offered were backed by third party guarantees and a further five by house guarantees. Three multi-million dollar offerings were withdrawn from the sale, including an Andy Warhol self portrait, estimated between $14m-$18m.

It wasn’t a perfect evening: six lots failed to sell. These included a small-scale group of seven Jackson Pollock paintings from the 1950s (est $7m-$9m); a 1915 Modigliani painting Beatrice Hastings sitting (est $5m-$7m); and a 1945 Léger canvas (est $1.2m-$1.8m). Including the three withdrawn lots, this amounted to an 88% sell through rate.

Still, six artist records were set, including the 11-ft high Fernando Botero bronze, Horse (2006), which was parked on the sidewalk in front of Christie’s Rockefeller Center headquarters, and made $4.2m ($5.2m with fees).

The marathon evening got off to a modest start with Mary Bauermeister’s wooden box construction packed with optical elements, Nature Mort (1967-69), which made $100,000 ($128,000 with fees), the first from the collection of investment banker and art scholar Herbert Lust.

The Lust trove of eight works (a Frank Stella estimated at $7m-$10m was withdrawn before the sale) realised $42m with fees, topped by Alberto Giacometti’s impossibly thin, 119cm-high bronze, Figure, demie grandeur (no.2) from 1949 that made $22m ($25.9m with fees), against an estimate of $20m-$30m.

Beyond Lust, a late and untitled Mark Rothko acrylic on paper laid down on canvas in fiery red hues from 1968 made $11.5m ($13.9m with fees) and Philip Guston’s feather light brush strokes in Painting from 1952 sold for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees), topping out the few Ab-Ex offerings.

The evening featured two mega-priced lots, both estimated at $60m-$80m. Wassily Kandinsky’s Weimar-era abstraction Betonte Ecken (accentuated corners, 1923), which once owned by the Guggenheim Museum co-founder Hilla Rebay, soared to a record $74m ($85.8m with fees). The anonymous seller acquired it at Sotheby’s New York in May 1986 for $1m.

Gustav Klimt’s dazzling lakeside composition, Litzlbergkeller from 1915-16, was observed and painted by Klimt with the aid of a telescope positioned and capturing the stout likeness of the Austrian inn he frequented for eight idyllic summers. It floated to $71m ($82.3m with fees).

Alex Rotter, Christie’s global president, nabbed both works for anonymous clients on his rainmaking telephone.

The Klimt had been acquired by last night's consignor at Sotheby’s New York in May 1997 from the estate of Neue Galerie co-founder Serge Sabarsky for a then-record $14.4m.

A standout of the season, Wilfredo Lam’s large, tropical-inspired composition executed in a Magical Realism style, Ogue Orisa (Eggue Orissa, l’herbe des dieux) from 1943, made a record $9.5m ($11.6m with fees). It debuted at the Pierre Matisse Gallery in 1944 and was recently featured in the Museum of Modern Art retrospective Wilfredo Lam: When I Don’t Sleep, I Dream. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s New York in November 1997 for $1.3m with fees. The Lam came to market backed by a third-party guarantee.

Impressionist era paintings were also in rich supply. Paul Cézanne’s luscious tabletop still life Tasse, verre et fruits (around 1877) was consigned by the 86-year-old billionaire businessman William I. Koch. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees).

The Cézanne was once owned by the former Dutch banker Siegfried Kramarsky, whose estate sold Vincent van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr Gachet from 1890 at Christie’s New York in May 1990 for a then-record $82.5m with fees.

French painting masters continued with Camille Pissarro’s evocative and crowded Parisian cityscape (sans protesters), Le Pont-Neuf, après-midi de pluie, 1re série from 1901 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees). It last sold at Christie’s New York in November 2019 for $6.5m with fees.

Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s Hercules and Achelous (1590)

Big name consignors were not in short supply as evidenced by a trove of Picassos and several Old Master works under the marketing title “Heroes & Lovers: Property of a Distinguished Collector”—also known as Jeff Koons.

The group was led by Picasso’s snogging couple, Le Baiser (October 1969), which is famed in part for its inclusion in the artist’s late paintings exhibition in Avignon at the Palais des Papes in 1970, and went for $26.5m ($31.1m with fees).

The monochrome composition depicting the artist and his wife and muse Jacqueline Roque conveys both passion and love in the artist’s last decade. Though a relatively big price, it came nowhere near its $40-$60m estimate.

Backed by a third-party guarantee, the work was acquired by Koons from Sotheby’s New York in May 2008 for $17.4m, the same year his Balloon flower-Magenta from 1995-2000 sold at Christies London for £12.9m, or $25.7m.

Picasso’s Tête de femme (Dora Maar), painted in wartime Paris on 25 May 1941 sold for $25.5m ($30m with fees). Another Dora Maar split-angle composition with her face featured alongside her rival Marie-Therese Walther from 1939-40 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees) against an unrealistic estimate of $10m-$15m.

The Koons trove, backed by third party guarantees also included a trio of Old Master works, topped by Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s dramatic, mythological depiction of Hercules and Achelous from 1590, and hugely scaled at 91.45cm by 242.57cm. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees), below its $12m-$18m estimate but enough to once again set the artist's record. Koons acquired it at Christie’s New York in April 2008 for a then-record $8.1 million. All in, the Koons group tallied $104.7m with fees.

Willem de Kooning’s rushing Yellow River from 1958, deaccessioned by the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York “to benefit the collection", and once described by the late critic Thomas B. Hess as “abstract parkway landscapes”, made $9m ($11m with fees).

One of the best back stories of the season came courtesy of Georgia O’Keeffe’s Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I (1930), which was found buried in a trunk by the niece of the East Village owner who received it as a college graduation present in 1963. Rarely does one see property titles from the East Village. One newspaper article said the elderly owner, a former Foreign Service member, decided to hide the painting away in the mid 1980s after one visitor eyed it and she grew suspicious.

It hasn’t been seen in public since 1931 when it was featured in Alfred Stieglitz’s An American Place gallery solo show of the artist. It made $3.9m ($4.8m with fees).

Another version of the curvy sand hills of the Rio Grande Valley composition where O’Keeffe had her studio sold at Christie’s New York in May 2018 from the collection of Peggy and David Rockefeller for $8.4m.

Though the Frida Kahlo painting Congreso de los pueblos por la paz (1952) was withdrawn at the 11th hour over export issues, her husband Diego Rivera fared better, with the floral Vendedora de flores, de Tehauntepec (1929) blossoming at $8.1m ($9.9m with fees). It blew past its $3.5m high estimate—another winner for the William I. Koch collection which all in realised $66.3m.

“It felt like a very calibrated evening with a solid but measured pace,” said Adrien Meyer, Christie’s auctioneer, as he exited the salesroom. “There was significant participation from Asia that I haven’t seen in a while.”

#9064. Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success

For decades, explanations for why some children struggle with reading have often focused on two factors: intelligence and the ability to process visual information. Children who read easily have frequently been assumed to be more intelligent, while those who struggle have sometimes been viewed as less capable. Another common belief is that reading difficulties arise primarily from problems interpreting the words and letters on a page.

However, a major new study challenges these assumptions, suggesting that the abilities most important for reading success may be very different from what many people expect.

Dr. Daniel Hajovsky, an associate professor in Texas A&M University's Department of Educational Psychology, led one of the most extensive investigations to date into how cognitive abilities relate to reading performance. The research brought together scientists from the University of Kansas, St. John's University, Montclair State University and Temple University to examine which mental skills best predict reading development and why some children encounter difficulties.

Massive Study Reveals What Really Predicts Reading Success

To investigate these relationships, the researchers combined 50,000 correlations drawn from 137 cognitive and achievement test batteries into a single statistical model. This large-scale approach allowed them to assess the contribution of individual mental abilities to reading performance while also helping clarify why previous studies had sometimes produced conflicting conclusions.

The findings revealed several surprises. Visual processing showed no meaningful relationship with reading ability across the analysis. General intelligence was associated with reading performance, but its influence was considerably smaller than some earlier research had suggested.

Instead, two less frequently discussed abilities emerged as particularly important predictors of reading success: auditory processing and comprehension-knowledge.

"One notable finding was that general intelligence was less dominant than in some earlier meta-analyses," Hajovsky said. "Broad abilities such as comprehension-knowledge and auditory processing played strong, specific roles in reading beyond general intelligence, especially for decoding and comprehension."

Two Overlooked Skills Play a Major Role in Reading

Auditory processing involves recognizing and distinguishing the individual sounds that make up spoken words. For example, a child needs to identify the separate sounds within a word to understand how those sounds correspond to written letters. This skill helps support decoding, the process of working out how written words are pronounced.

Comprehension-knowledge refers to the vocabulary, concepts and background information a child has accumulated through learning and everyday experiences. Having this foundation makes it easier to understand the meaning of words, sentences and longer passages.

Together, these two abilities were more reliable predictors of reading performance than any other skills examined in the study. Other cognitive functions, including memory, reasoning and mental processing speed, also contributed to reading development, although they played more supporting roles.

The results suggest that reading is not simply a reflection of overall intelligence or how effectively a child processes visual information. Instead, it depends on several interconnected abilities, with language-related skills playing especially important roles.

What the Findings Mean for Children Who Struggle to Read

The research could help educators better understand why individual students experience reading difficulties. Rather than treating all reading problems as the same, teachers may be able to identify particular weaknesses and provide instruction that addresses those needs.

For families, the findings also offer an encouraging message. A child who has trouble reading is not necessarily less intelligent or incapable of becoming a strong reader. Difficulties may instead reflect specific abilities that need additional development and support.

"Strengthening foundational skills at home, even the ones that seem simple, can have meaningful effects on more advanced reading abilities," Hajovsky said. "Struggles in reading are not a sign of low ability but often reflect one specific skill that needs strengthening within a larger system that works together."

The findings highlight the value of helping children build essential reading skills through consistent support, both in the classroom and at home.

According to Hajovsky, the most effective approach involves cooperation among schools, parents, and communities. Reading develops through a network of connected skills, and strengthening those foundations one step at a time can help children become more confident and capable readers.

Materials provided by Texas A&M University. Original written by Ryan McCullar. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9063. When Your Doctor Prescribes a Visit to an Art Gallery

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

The soulful deep greens and browns of British Columbia’s forests weave together with ferns and moss, catching the light through the tops of ancient firs and cedars. The trees sway, and the earth rises and falls among the rocks.

But in this case, the view isn’t from the trail. It is a painting by Canadian artist Emily Carr on display in the Vancouver Art Gallery, and some of those who are experiencing it are doing so because it was prescribed by their health care provider. How they ended up there is the result of a bit of creative thinking that honors the role of art in healing.

In 2025, the gallery partnered with BC Parks Foundation to extend PaRx, Canada’s national nature prescription program, to include the gallery. PaRx is a successful initiative that has included an estimated 2 million prescriptions issued by more than 20,000 health care providers. Typically, these prescriptions are for time outdoors, with added benefits, like free transportation, to reduce barriers to access.   Using art as an entry point into nature as a formal intervention is novel—the first collaboration of its kind between a nature prescription program and an arts institution in the world, according to Sirish Rao, the gallery’s co-CEO and executive director. While art-based prescriptions are gaining in popularity, this program goes a step further, integrating engagement with nature in a gentle, accessible way. Other institutions around the world are looking to the Vancouver Art Gallery program as a model initiative that can be replicated in other communities to support people’s well-being.

The process starts when a health care provider like a doctor, nurse, or therapist determines that a patient might benefit from a prescription to spend time in nature, including around the nature-inspired visual art at the gallery. The benefits can be many: combating isolation, engaging mentally and physically during a gallery visit, and experiencing awe and beauty.

The prescription to Vancouver Art Gallery includes free admission for the prescription holder and a guest, as well as a printed guide that offers prompts and questions to consider—for example, to notice the varied shades of green Carr used, or imagine a walk along a trail she painted—along with research about the benefits of experiencing nature. Participants are guided through “slow looking” as the act of learning through observation, imagination exercises, and physical movement—yes, swaying in an art gallery is encouraged.

After the visit, guests are invited to continue the immersion at a local nature space, with free carshare minutes to get there if needed. The art prescription guide suggests nearby parks where participants can walk or hike, extending slow looking from a curated indoor experience to the outdoors if they choose. And they can return to the gallery as often as they like by retaining their original prescription. On site, they can join free workshops, and a coloring book offers a contemplative experience at home.

This is an example of social prescribing, a worldwide movement that serves as a complement to clinical care and typical medication prescriptions by prescribing from a wide range of activities that support physical and mental health. Beyond art galleries and nature walks, this can include music classes, exercise sessions, or gardening programs.  The prescription is personal and can be tailored to patients’ needs and interests.

Carla Fry is a West Vancouver psychologist and educator with more than 20 years of clinical experience. She says the art gallery prescription has been a gift for participants, especially those who face physical, mental, social, or even financial or transportation barriers to accessing nature. Many are surprised that they don’t have to pay anything for the experience.

“For them to understand that so many people have come together to create this opportunity, I think that in and of itself is special,” Fry says. “They say, ‘Wow, my community cares.’ The possibility that this exists, it’s available, it’s free—there’s something about that . . . that’s noteworthy.”

Fry is one of the professionals who gives these kinds of prescriptions to her clients. It’s another tool available to promote well-being.

“Of course, I’m never telling them to go. We talk about this as a prescription, but I always present it as ‘here’s an opportunity to meet some of your goals, and here’s what the opportunity looks like,’” she says.

As yet, no one has declined her prescription.

“They’re surprised that something so seemingly simplistic as slowing down and really looking, really living in front of the art or in nature is actually an intervention,” Fry says. “People in our culture are set up to think that growth has got to be painful, growth has got to be difficult, growth has got to be expensive, growth is going to take a long time. When I bring forward an intervention of going to a location, and your job as a client of mine is to appreciate, the first reaction is surprise. It opens up an entire conversation—‘I can just appreciate my life and not always be grinding to make it better.’ It’s a special process for me to witness.”

The goal is to do more than increase the number of people who have exposure to art, though that might be a side effect. The formal prescription to nature through art is designed to reduce stress, anxiety, and social isolation. The ability to bring a guest, as well as the opportunity to experience art with other patrons, is key.

“There are other people there; these aren’t private viewings. But of course, sometimes people don’t feel connected to others in a room. Sometimes they do; sometimes it’s enough to feel that they’re part of a community. But others really benefit from being able to have a shared experience where they can reflect in real time and reflect afterwards,” Fry says.

Paula Toledo is the mental health advisor and lead well-being consultant at Vancouver Art Gallery, leading the Richardson Family Art of Wellbeing Lab. The lab aims to connect the community to art as a means to improve mental and physical well-being, drawing on a collaboration of researchers, scientists, physicians, and Indigenous Elders and healers.

Toledo came to this work through the personal experience of losing her husband and her mother within months, while also caring for her newborn child. That grief and her recovery changed the course of her life and her career in wellness.

“When we encounter something so vast that it transcends our current understanding of the world, it can be very mysterious,” Toledo says:

Sometimes it can be a very positive experience, but other times, like in cases of grief, it can also make you stop and wonder about the mystery behind it. I was in awe and I remember that exact moment where I thought, “Well, if that could happen, then the opposite must also be true.” That’s what the research supports: When we experience awe, it can lead to wonder, which is this mental state of openness and curiosity. Every day I woke up with that sense of curiosity that this might be the day that I turn the corner and collide with good fortune. That experience was so transformative that it led me to actually seek out resources.

Toledo’s health care provider connected her with a social worker who prescribed movement and art in the form of yoga and music classes.

I started to feel more energized and connected to my own self-determination,” she says. “If we look at the research on why social prescribing is so impactful, it’s because it really does encourage self-determination. I started to feel more connected to my community, more connected to my children, connecting to their own wonder, and it became this upward spiral towards healing and towards rebuilding my life.”

Monica Harrison is one of the many prescription holders who has learned to lean into the peace and beauty of slowing down through the program. She is an educational assistant who works with students with support needs and advocates for their inclusion in schools. She experienced health issues that required her to be on leave from work and that triggered depression and anxiety.

“I’m neurodivergent, so I’m autistic and I have ADHD. I’ve had anxiety my whole life, and I’ve learned a lot of coping mechanisms that help me to control that. But with undiagnosed conditions that have been going on, it has awoken a lot of anxiety, and it makes it hard to manage my mood,” she says.

Harrison met Toledo, who introduced her to the prescription program. What started with Harrison’s immersion in art has resulted in her increasing use of the program in other locations, both indoors and out.

Harrison, who enjoys nature photography, says she was introduced to Carr’s paintings in elementary school, and she fell in love with the local subject matter. Now as an adult, that connection to art has opened new opportunities.

“When we visited the gallery, I was able to discuss paintings and identify what I was feeling. It really allowed me to label what I was feeling more accurately and then think about it. Just through her artwork, it really made me feel nurturing and protection,” she says.

Through other exhibitions at the gallery, Harrison says she found surprise and joy and “a lot of beautiful sensory feelings to my mind and my body and my soul”:

Chronic illnesses [have] made my life very small, with a lot of losses that come with the territory, such as giving up things that I once enjoyed like working, walking in nature, seeing friends, traveling. I found the prescription to be very flexible. You can do it whenever you’re able to. It can give you something specific to try out. You can do it on your own. You can do it with friends and family, and I think it’s a great thing for people with chronic illness. And it can also give those people a practical way to learn how nature connects to positive mental health. It can be something they can build on through a positive experience with their prescription . . . and add to their toolkit.

Fry says she hears two recurring themes from prescription holders: Experiencing art feels immersive, and the process of visiting the gallery—from the prescription as an invitation to the encouragement to engage in “slow looking”—is a special event that makes them feel cared for.

“It’s something different. It’s something novel. It’s something fresh,” she says, whereas doing the same gratitude practices over and over can get repetitive. “It’s a lot more powerful when we add novel opportunities or events or experiences to our practice. For every person that I’ve prescribed this to, it’s been new to them, so it hits that mark really nicely,” she says.

Art, nature, music, dance, and other social prescriptions have decades of demonstrated success. Toledo points to social prescribing in the U.K. as an example where community connectors or social workers serve as entry points for patients to discover what activities might be meaningful to them. For some, that might mean a return to an activity they enjoyed in years past, like Toledo’s own reengagement with music during her grief.

The social prescription movement continues to gain ground, with providers taking notice at a growing pace. It requires community, collaboration, and a foundation of care that looks at health through a wide lens. In the United States, organizations like Social Prescribing USA are championing the effort as a medical intervention.

For Rao, the impact extends far beyond people’s visits to the gallery.

“What we’re looking at is a way of seeing,” Rao says. “That way of seeing then applies to anything.”

Chris Worthy is an award-winning freelance writer and editor who believes every person has a story to tell. Her background in law led to a career in writing that has spanned more than 25 years.

By focusing on culture, family, and community, Jasmin Brooks Stephens says we can support mental health in Black youth long before crises occur.

In three years, I lost five loved ones, my dog, my childhood home, and my sense of invincibility. What I gained was a deeper capacity for gratitude.

According to an analysis of 99 studies, mental well-being leads to a longer life.

What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.

What if you could fall in love, or forge deep connections, in just 45 minutes? Our guests, Kristen Meinzer and Jolenta Greenberg of By The Book podcast, try out 36 questions with their partners to see if they can strengthen their connection.

The Greater Good Science Center studies the psychology, sociology, and neuroscience of well-being, and teaches skills that foster a thriving, resilient, and compassionate society.

#9062. Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired

Why does the left side of the brain control the right side of the body, while the right side controls the left? This unusual arrangement is one of the most intriguing features of the nervous system, and scientists have proposed a new explanation that reaches back hundreds of millions of years.

Dr. Martin Wessendorf, a neuroscientist and associate professor emeritus at the University of Minnesota, studies how the brainstem regulates neurons in the spinal cord. Daniel Wang specializes in cognitive neuroscience and neurodegenerative diseases. Together, they have examined the evolutionary origins of the brain's crossed connections.

In a study published in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, the researchers explore several neural circuits in four-limbed animals that are cross-wired (meaning one side of the brain connects with the opposite side of the body). Their hypothesis suggests that these connections may have developed because evolution built new brain circuits around an ancient visual system.

The brain contains numerous pathways that cross from one side of the central nervous system to the other. Understanding why these contralateral (midline-crossing) connections exist requires examining how different sensory and movement circuits developed over evolutionary time.

How the Brain Processes Visual Information

One possible explanation begins with the eyes. When light passes through the eye's lens, the image projected onto the retina is reversed. Objects appearing to our right are projected onto the left side of the retina, while objects on our left are projected onto the right.

Visual information travels along the optic nerve to a structure called the optic chiasm. Here, nerve fibers are organized so that information from the right visual field reaches the left side of the brain, while information from the left visual field is directed to the right side.

Some of these signals reach an ancient brain structure called the optic tectum (which in mammals is called the superior colliculus). Located in the midbrain, this region helps produce fast reactions to visual events, such as suddenly noticing something moving nearby.

Each side of the optic tectum contains a representation of the opposite visual field. Deeper within the structure, information about physical sensations (somatosensory information) is also organized into corresponding maps.

Because the optic tectum exists in every vertebrate species, it is considered one of the most ancient structures in the vertebrate nervous system. Its early appearance may be especially important for understanding why so many other neural pathways cross sides.

Why Sensory Signals Cross the Brain and Spinal Cord

The researchers also examined two major pathways responsible for transmitting sensations from the body to the brain. Both cross the center of the central nervous system (the brain and spinal cord), and both appear to be widespread among tetrapods (the animals with four limbs, including mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians).

The first, called the dorsal column pathway, carries information about gentle touch, vibration, and the position of different body parts. Signals from the limbs and torso travel upward through the dorsal portion of the spinal cord before reaching another neuron in the brainstem, just above the spinal cord. From there, the pathway crosses to the opposite side.

Although fish lack this pathway, scientists have identified it in amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Its presence across these major animal groups suggests that the arrangement emerged early in tetrapod evolution and has remained largely conserved.

The second pathway, known as the spinothalamic tract, transmits sensations involving pain, itching, and certain types of touch. Unlike the dorsal column pathway, it crosses to the opposite side within the spinal cord itself.

After crossing, signals travel upward to the thalamus, a brain region located above the midbrain that plays a central role in processing sensory and movement information.

This crossed arrangement is found in birds, mammals, and reptiles. It also occurs in some cartilaginous fish, including sharks and rays, suggesting that aspects of this organization have even deeper evolutionary roots.

How the Brain Controls Movement Across the Body

The crossed organization of the nervous system extends beyond sensation. The researchers identified three important pathways involved in controlling skeletal muscles that also connect one side of the brain with the opposite side of the spinal cord.

The first is the tectospinal pathway, which helps the body respond rapidly to information from the environment.

The optic tectum processes more than vision. It also receives information about sounds and physical sensations, organizing these signals into maps that align with its visual representation on the opposite side of the brain.

Imagine preparing to cross a street when you suddenly notice a car approaching from the corner of your eye. You instinctively turn toward the vehicle. The tectospinal pathway is one of the neural circuits that helps produce this rapid response. It can also coordinate similar reactions to unexpected sounds or touch.

The movement signals originate in the deepest layers of the optic tectum and travel through nerve fibers to the opposite side of the spinal cord. This pathway is present in most tetrapods and certain cartilaginous fish.

Another important circuit is the rubrospinal pathway, which is thought to help animals control their limbs. It begins in a midbrain structure called the red nucleus and extends to the opposite side of the spinal cord. The pathway is especially prominent in most mammals, although it has also been identified in other tetrapods and some cartilaginous fish.

The Evolution of Fine Motor Control in Humans

The third pathway, called the corticospinal tract, has a particularly important role in humans because it supports precise movements, including the fine control of our fingers.

Its evolutionary history is more complicated than that of the other pathways.

All vertebrates possess a telencephalon, the forward portion of the brain that accounts for much of the brain's overall size in humans. However, only mammals have a cerebral cortex organized into six distinct layers.

This six-layered cortex supports sophisticated functions such as combining sensory information with memories, coordinating movement, and processing language.

The corticospinal pathway extends from the cerebral cortex toward the spinal cord, but its function varies among animals.

In most mammals, it primarily influences sensory processing. Nerve fibers reach spinal cord regions that receive information from the body, allowing the brain to regulate incoming sensations.

In primates (including humans) and certain other animals capable of highly precise movements, the pathway also reaches spinal cord regions responsible for controlling muscles. These connections make intricate actions possible, including the coordinated finger movements needed for delicate tasks.

Depending on the species, the corticospinal tract can regulate sensory information or contribute directly to movement. In either case, its fibers cross the midline of the nervous system.

The researchers suggest that humans may have developed advanced fine motor abilities by adapting an older neural circuit originally involved in controlling sensory input. Rather than creating an entirely new system, evolution may have given an existing pathway an additional purpose.

A 500-Million-Year-Old Explanation for the Brain's Crossed Wiring

Taken together, these neural pathways point toward a potentially surprising explanation for the brain's unusual organization.

The researchers propose that the earliest visual circuits helped establish a pattern in which sensory and movement pathways were organized across opposite sides of the nervous system. Later circuits may have inherited this arrangement as they evolved, particularly in tetrapods.

Because every living vertebrate possesses an optic chiasm and an optic tectum organized around information from the opposite visual field, the researchers suspect that these structures were already present in primitive jawless fish during the Cambrian Period, approximately 538 to 486 million years ago.

If correct, this would mean that the basic organization underlying the brain's crossed connections began developing more than half a billion years before modern humans appeared.

The hypothesis may even be testable. Scientists could examine fossilized skulls from ancient jawless fish for anatomical evidence that might help establish whether these early animals possessed an optic chiasm and optic tectum.

An Evolutionary Inheritance Rather Than an Advantage?

The broader idea challenges the assumption that every unusual biological feature must have evolved because it provided a direct survival benefit.

Evolution often modifies structures that already exist instead of developing completely new systems. Once the ancient visual pathways established a crossed organization, that arrangement may have influenced how additional sensory and motor circuits developed.

In particular, the organization of the visual system (and in particular, the optic tectum) may have provided a structural foundation that later pathways followed.

Under this hypothesis, the brain's crossed connections did not necessarily arise because controlling the opposite side of the body was inherently more effective. Instead, they may reflect the lasting influence of an ancient arrangement that evolution repeatedly reused.

The result could be one of the most enduring examples of how the nervous system preserves its evolutionary history. The strange relationship between the brain's two hemispheres and the opposite sides of the body may ultimately trace back to the visual systems of animals that lived more than 500 million years ago.

#9061. Heart, the Heretic: The Forgotten Visionary Jane Ellen Harrison on Critical Thinking, Emotional Imagination, and How to Fix the World

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If it makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider aiding its sustenance with a one-time or loyal donation. Your support makes all the difference.

You can also become a spontaneous supporter with a one-time donation in any amount:

Partial to Bitcoin? You can beam some bit-love my way: 197usDS6AsL9wDKxtGM6xaWjmR5ejgqem7

Need to cancel a recurring donation? Go here.

For an act of resistance to the tyranny of algorithms, try the Marginalian newsletter—undistracted notes on the search for meaning, free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human since 2006. (Here is an example.)

UPDATE 2025: This book is now back in print as the third title in Marginalian Editions.

When the Inquisition persecuted Galileo for advancing the rude truth that Earth is not the center of the universe, the charge against him was heresy — the same charge on which Joan of Arc was burned at the stake for her crusade for political reform. We have had many words for heretics over the epochs — rebels, radicals, freethinkers — but they have always been the ones to dislodge humanity from the stagnation of the status quo, to illuminate our blind spots, dismantle our unexamined biases, and jolt us out of our herd mentality. Without those devoted to seeing reality more clearly and possibility more wildly, we would still live in a world haunted by superstition and governed by dogma.

The power and dignity of this most courageous human mindset is what the pioneering classicist Jane Ellen Harrison (September 9, 1850–April 15, 1928), who brought the culture of Ancient Greece to the modern world, explores in her magnificent essay “Heresy and Humanity,” found in Alpha and Omega (public library) — the out-of-print essay collection that gave us Harrison on the art of growing older, published just as humanity was being dehumanized by its first World War.

The word “heretic” has still about it an emotional thrill — a glow reflected, it may be, from the fires at Smithfield, the ardours of those who were burnt at the stake for the love of an idea.

Heresy, the Greek hairesis, was from the outset an eager, living word. The taking of a city, its expugnatio, is a hairesis; the choosing of a lot in life or an opinion, its electio, is a hairesis; always in the word hairesis there is this reaching out to grasp, this studious, zealous pursuit — always something personal, even passionate… To be a heretic today is almost a human obligation.

In a sentiment Bertrand Russell would echo in timeless manifesto for freedom of thought, Harrison adds:

The gist of heresy is free personal choice in act, and specifically in thought — the rejection of traditional faiths and customs.

A century and a half after Emerson inveighed that “masses are rude, lame, unmade, pernicious in their demands and influence,” she considers what makes heresy so difficult yet so necessary to the health of society:

All traditional views are held with such tenacity, such almost ferocity, because they belong to the class of views induced, not by individual experience, still less by reason, but by collective, or, as it is sometimes called “herd,” suggestion. This used to be called “faith.” The belief so held may or may not be true; collective suggestion is not in the least necessarily collective hallucination. Mere collective suggestions — that is the interesting point — have the quality of obviousness; they do not issue from the individual, but seem imposed from outside, and ineluctable; they have all the inevitableness of instinctive opinion… Hence they are held with an intensity of emotion far beyond any reasoned conviction. To doubt them is felt to be at once idiocy and irreverence. Inquiry into their rational bases is naturally, and in a sense rightly, resented, because they are not rationally based, though they may be rationally supported. It is by convictions such as this that a society of the homogenous kind — a society based on and held together by uniformity — lives and thrives. To attack them is to cripple and endanger its inmost life.

Observing that the development of science is what pivoted heresy from damnable to desirable in society, Harrison contrasts sensemaking by empiricism with sensemaking by authority:

Science classifies, draws ever clearer distinctions; herd-suggestion is always in a haze. Herd-suggestion is all for tradition, authority; science has for its very essence the exercise of free thought. So long as we will not take the trouble to know exactly and intimately, we may not — must not — choose… We must follow custom; we must accept the mandates of [those] who enforce tradition.

Science opens wide the doors that turned so slowly on tradition’s hinges, and opens them on clean, quiet places where we breathe larger air… It is well to remember our debt to science — our inward and spiritual as well as material debt.

And yet, Harrison argues, the heretic needs more than science — the heretic needs humanity. She writes:

Science broke the binding spell of herd-suggestion. For that great boon let us now and ever bless and praise her holy name. She cleared the collective haze, she drew sharp distinctions, appealing to individual actual experience, to individual powers of reasoning. But by neither individual sense — perception nor ratiocination alone do we live. Our keenest emotional life is through the herd, and hence it was that, at the close of the last century, the flame of scientific hope, the glory of scientific individualism that had blazed so brightly, somehow died down and left a strange chill. Man rose up from the banquet of reason and law unfed. He hungered half unconsciously for the herd. It seemed an impasse: on the one side orthodoxy, tradition, authority, practical slavery; on the other science, individual freedom, reason, and an aching loneliness.

We live now just at the transition moment; we have broken with the old, we have not quite adjusted ourselves to the new. It is not so much the breaking with the old faiths that makes us restless as the living in a new social structure.

At the root of this new social structure, she observes, is not the old cult of homogeneity but the recognition of individuality, and the diversity of individualities, as the wellspring of vitality and social harmony — “differentiation that would unite, not divide.” With the World War flaming around her, waged on the herd-versus-herd collision of nationalisms and ideologies, she writes:

Only through and by this organic individuality can the real sense and value of Humanity emerge. We are humane so far as we are conscious or sensitive to individual life. Patriotism is collective herd-instinct; it is repressive of individuality. You feel strongly because you feel alike; you are reinforced by the other homogenous unites; you sing the same song and wave the same flag. Humanity is sympathy with infinite differences, with utter individualism, with complete differentiation, and it is only possible through the mystery of organic spiritual union. We have come, most of us, now, to a sort of physical union by sympathy and imagination. To torture even an enemy’s body would be to us physical pain, physical sickness. There will come the day when to hurt mentally and spiritually will be equally impossible, because the spiritual life will by enhanced sympathy be one. But this union is only possible through that organic differentiation that makes us have need one of the other.

A generation before Albert Camus, in the midst of the next World War, called for the superhuman duty to “mend what has been torn apart, make justice imaginable again in a world so obviously unjust, give happiness a meaning once,” Harrison concludes:

In a word, if we are to be true and worthy heretics, we need not only new heads, but new hearts, and, most of all, that new emotional imagination, joint offspring of head and heart which is begotten of enlarged sympathies and a more sensitive habit of feeling. About the moral problem there is nothing mysterious; it is simply the old, old question of how best to live together. We no longer believe in an unchanging moral law imposed from without. We know that a harder incumbency is upon us; we must work out our law from within.

Noting that we have outgrown the easy shorthand for morality offered by religious dogma, she contours what is asked of us if we are to rehumanize humanity:

We must adventure a harder and higher spiritual task… a steady and even ardent recognition of the individual life, in its infinite variety, with its infinite interactions. We decline to be ourselves part of an undifferentiated mass; we refuse to deal with others in classes and masses… We are dissatisfied now not only with the herd-sanctions of religion, but with many of those later sanctities of law to which some even emancipated thinkers ascribe a sort of divinity. We feel the inherent savagery of law in that it treats individuals as masses… Yet all the time we know that we can, with spiritual safety, rebel only in so far as we are personally sensitive to the claims of other individual lives that touch our own. The old herd-problem remains of how to live together; and as the union grows closer and more intricate the chances of mutual hurt are greater, and the sensitiveness must grow keener. Others are safe from and with us only when their pain is our pain, their joy ours.

Couple with E.E. Cummings on the courage to feel, then revisit Albert Camus on what it means to be a rebel, the radical Russian dissident prince Peter Kropotkin on the spirit of revolt, and the pioneering X-ray crystallographer and peace activist Kathleen Lonsdale on moral courage and our personal power in world change.

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. #9060. Della Robbia relief at the Frick Collection gets a crucial upgrade

The recently studied Della Robbia in its new location, the museum's Octagon Room, The Frick Collection, New York Photo: Joseph Coscia Jr.

For a good part of the 15th and 16th centuries, Florentine sculptors named Della Robbia were making glazed terracotta works of great renown. But not all Della Robbias were created equal. Scholars and collectors have long given strong preference to Luca della Robbia (1399/1400-1482), the founder of the dynasty, and his nephew Andrea della Robbia (1435-1525). Similar works by later Della Robbias and those produced by the workshop can come in a very distant third. For decades, New York’s Frick Collection believed it owned a relief by the family workshop, dated no earlier than the 16th century. But now, after technical analysis and consultation with experts in the field, the museum has updated its Virgin and Child to a 15th-century original, likely from the 1470s or 80s.

“We’re suggesting it’s by Andrea,” says Greta Llanes Serrano, a conservation fellow at the Frick who worked on the recent treatment that helped pinpoint the new attribution.

The framed relief depicts a veiled Madonna holding a Christ child, attended by cherubs. Fashioned out of buff-coloured earthenware, it has the Della Robbia clan’s distinctive white and blue glazes, with, in this case, traces of gilding. The work was first acquired by Helen Clay Frick, Henry’s daughter, in 1922 and spent most of the last century stashed outside the main reading room of the Frick Art Research Library.

Greta Llanes Serrano treating the Frick's Della Robbia in the Frick Collection's newly built Sherman Fairchild Center for Art Conservation Photo: George Koelle

Llanes Serrano says the road to the new attribution was filled with twists and turns, and an outright gap or two.

The early American luminary in Della Robbia studies was the Princeton University art historian Allan Marquand (1853-1924). Llanes Serrano says that in a 1906 publication Marquand identified the work, then in the possession of a private German collector, as being by either Luca or “very early Andrea”. Then, in 1914, he decided “that it had to be Andrea”. After it landed in the Frick family collection and found its way to the library entrance, it went from being a Della Robbia, generally, she says, to a work by Andrea—a decision, she notes, recorded by a librarian, though who actually made the decision is not known. Later, it was outright demoted to “school of Della Robbia” and has had that lower-rung status since at least 2008.

Julia Day, who was appointed last year as the Frick’s new chief conservator, thought it was time to take a new look at the work after attending a Della Robbia conference in spring 2025. “I just thought that we have this piece, and nobody’s really spent time looking at it,” Day says.

Llanes Serrano, who analysed the relief over the last year in the Frick’s new conservation studio, says XRF analysisallowed her to move back the dating and place it closer to Andrea himself. “I took multiple readings on different spots on the back and front,” she says, of the non-invasive technique.

Greta Llanes Serrano treating the frame of the Frick's Della Robbia in the Frick Collection's newly built Sherman Fairchild Center for Art Conservation Photo: George Koelle

The process revealed the elements present in the glaze, and then she compared her results with other analyses of autograph Della Robbia works. This helped her to place it in the new 1470s-80s time frame, when the older Luca was giving way to the younger Andrea. Meanwhile, another clue was plainly visible: “The Christ Child is clothed,” she says. In later versions of the motif made by the sculptors and their workshop, she adds, it was more common to show him unclothed.

A few weeks ago, the museum moved the work away from the library, where it was out of view from the general public, and installed it in a damask-lined spot in the mansion’s first-floor Octagon Room, fresh from its makeover during the Frick’s recent renovation.

Day says this kind of conservation-guided upgrade is a rarity at the Frick, happening perhaps once a decade. The Virgin and Child is the only Della Robbia piece in the museum's collection, she adds.

The Frick veteran is particularly excited about all the new conservation spaces, created as part of the museum’s recent Selldorf-designed expansion

Evocative surprises await: while its Gilded Age home is closed for renovation and expansion, the Frick displays its masterworks in austere Modernist surroundings on Madison Avenue

With 83% of its renovation fund raised, the museum is on target to reopen in its historic home in late 2024

Amsterdam’s Rijksmuseum is returning the favour and lending one of its works after showing the Frick’s Vermeers in its blockbuster exhibition last year
